video.title: Passwords nobody can guess
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student

scenes.visual: Computer room. Mr Joseph holds a phone showing a student's profile: a name at the top, a birthday cake photo below.
scenes.animation: Speech bubble pops; the profile slides up on the phone.
scenes.narration: A student once told me, “My password is safe: it’s my name and my birth year.” Then I opened his profile. His name was at the top. And right below it, a photo of his birthday cake.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: how passwords get guessed, and how to make one nobody can guess.

scenes.visual: A key opens a game, a chat and an email. A small robot fires guesses at a lock: 123456, names, birthdays, team names.
scenes.animation: Guess cards fly at the lock one after another.
scenes.on_screen_text: Programs try the easy guesses first
scenes.narration: A password is the key to your games, your chats and your email. Accounts aren’t broken into by people guessing by hand. Programs try millions of guesses: popular ones like one two three four five six, names, birthdays and football teams.

scenes.visual: A combination lock grows from three dials to six; a counter jumps from a thousand to a million. A 'P@ssw0rd' card bounces off a robot that already knows the trick.
scenes.animation: Dials add one by one; the counter rolls.
scenes.on_screen_text: Every extra character multiplies the work
scenes.narration: What slows them down is length. A lock with three dials has a thousand combinations; with six dials, a million. Every extra character multiplies the work. And swapping a letter for a symbol? Programs know that trick too.

scenes.visual: Clean card: three word tiles join into one long passphrase.
scenes.narration: Here’s the answer: a passphrase. Pick three or four random words that have nothing to do with you, and join them. It’s long, hard to guess and easy to picture.

scenes.visual: A silly picture: a bicycle loaded with mangoes rides through a thunderstorm, a spoon for a bell.
scenes.animation: Each word draws its part of the picture.
scenes.on_screen_text: Picture it, then make your own
scenes.narration: Mango, bicycle, thunder, spoon. Picture a bicycle full of mangoes in a thunderstorm, with a spoon for a bell. You won’t forget it. Just don’t use ours: make your own.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up three password cards.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Three passwords: a name with a year, the word password with symbols, and four random words. Which is hardest for a program to guess?

scenes.visual: The four-words card gets a check; the other two get crosses.
scenes.narration: Four random words. They’re long, and they say nothing about you. The other two are among the very first guesses a program tries.

scenes.visual: A game website leaks one password; arrows carry it to an email and a chat app. Reset links fly into the email.
scenes.narration: One password for everything is risky too. If one game website leaks it, criminals try it on your email and your chats. Your email matters most, because reset links go there. So every account gets its own password.

scenes.visual: Two friends; one hides a phone screen with a smile. A notebook goes into a drawer at home. A café computer shows a 'Sign out' button.
scenes.narration: Keep passwords secret, even from your best friend: friends fall out, and phones get borrowed. A parent or guardian who helps with your accounts is different. Too many to remember? Use a password manager, or a notebook kept safe at home. On a shared or café computer, always sign out.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph shows a chat: a friend asks for a game password to collect daily rewards.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Your best friend wants your game password, to collect your daily rewards while you’re away. Do you share it?

scenes.visual: Three summary cards: long, different, secret.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Keep it to yourself: a day of rewards isn’t worth your account. Remember: long random words, a different password for every account, and never shared.

scenes.visual: A student at home draws a funny scene in a notebook, then changes the email password with a parent beside them.
scenes.animation: Doodle draws itself; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: pick four random words and picture one funny scene that links them. If you still remember it at bedtime, make a new passphrase of your own for your email, with a parent’s help if you like.

checkpoints.prompt: Which password is hardest for a guessing program to crack?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — four random words are long and say nothing about you.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a name with a year, and symbols in place of letters, are among the first guesses. Four random words are much longer.

checkpoints.prompt: Your best friend wants your game password to collect your daily rewards. Do you share it?

options.text: No — passwords stay secret, even from friends

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a shared password can be passed on, used in a fight, or leaked. Friendship doesn’t need your password.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — friends fall out and phones get borrowed. Keep it secret, and miss a day of rewards instead.
